_about: Signal database for ../scripts/lib-fingerprint.py.
Every entry here is a PACKAGE-NAME BOUNDARY: a point where a library
renamed or relocated its package, so that the name alone constrains the
version. README section 3.7 technique 2 rates this the strongest of the
class-set signals, because a rename is a hard boundary rather than a
similarity score, and because library packages survive R8 (the SDK's own
consumer-rules.pro keeps them).
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN HERE
Exact version-to-class mappings. 'Class Foo was added in 4.7.2' is only
worth writing down if you verified it against the artifacts, and a
wrong entry here silently produces a wrong version number in somebody's
report. Use --refs with real JARs downloaded from Maven for that: the
script compares against the artifacts themselves, so it cannot be stale.
CVE data. This file says what a library IS, never whether it is
vulnerable. See ../faq.md on why an outdated library is not a finding.
HOW TO EXTEND IT
Add entries as you work. README section 8.1 Phase 2 is right that this
becomes one of your most valuable personal assets. Two rules:
1. every rule carries a 'source' saying how you know it;
2. if you cannot write that sentence, you do not know it yet.
kind: 'class_prefix'    classes exist directly under this package
kind: 'class_relocated' the package appears as an inner segment of some
other package -- a shaded copy, which a prefix
search would never find
bound: exact | min | max | presence
confidence: high | medium | low

rules.source: OkHttp 2.x lived under com.squareup.okhttp. Version 3 moved the whole library to the okhttp3 package precisely so both majors could coexist in one app. Seeing the old package is therefore an upper bound.
rules.raises: Confirm with --prefix com.squareup.okhttp --refs, using 2.x JARs from Maven Central.

rules.source: The okhttp3 package name was introduced with the 3.0 release and is still used by 4.x and 5.x. It narrows the major, not the minor.
rules.raises: Grep the DEX for the okhttp/x.y.z User-Agent fragment (T1), then run --prefix okhttp3 --refs to bracket the minor.

rules.source: Vendors that embed OkHttp routinely relocate it under their own namespace so that it cannot clash with the app's own copy. The relocated classes are byte-for-byte the same library.
rules.raises: Diff the relocated class set against real OkHttp releases; the shape will match even though the names do not.

rules.source: Okio is OkHttp's I/O layer and is pulled in transitively by it, by Retrofit, and by Moshi. Its presence without okhttp3 means something else brought it.
rules.raises: Find what depends on it: ./gradlew dependencyInsight if you have the build, otherwise look at which packages reference okio classes.

rules.source: Shaded alongside OkHttp by the same vendors, for the same reason.
rules.raises: Check whether the shaded copy and a non-shaded copy are BOTH present. Two copies of the same library at different versions is a real and reportable condition.

rules.source: AndroidX replaced the android.support.* namespace as the support-library successor. A build using it is on the modern artifact line.
rules.raises: META-INF/androidx.*.version stamps (T5) give literal per-artifact versions and are usually present in the same APK.

rules.source: The android.support.* namespace was frozen when AndroidX took over; nothing new ships under it. Its presence dates the dependency set.
rules.raises: Both namespaces in one APK usually means Jetifier or an un-migrated third-party AAR. Worth reporting as a maintenance observation, not a vulnerability.

rules.source: Crashlytics shipped under com.crashlytics.* in its Fabric incarnation, before the move to the Firebase artifact line.
rules.raises: Check the merged manifest for the matching initialisation provider; the authority names the era too.

rules.source: The Firebase artifact uses the com.google.firebase.crashlytics package.
rules.raises: Look for the com.google.firebase.crashlytics.* version stamp in META-INF.

rules.source: The vendor rebranded from Appboy to Braze and renamed the SDK package accordingly. Classes still under com.appboy predate that rename.
rules.raises: Both packages present at once is normal during a migration release; check which one the manifest's provider points at.

rules.source: The current package name.
rules.raises: Endpoint strings in the DEX corroborate the vendor independently of the package name.

rules.source: ExoPlayer 2 used com.google.android.exoplayer2. Its successor ships as AndroidX Media3 under androidx.media3.
rules.raises: ExoPlayer contains media parsers. Once identified, the question that matters is which extractors are reachable, not the version alone.

rules.source: Media3 is the AndroidX continuation of ExoPlayer.
rules.raises: META-INF/androidx.media3.*.version stamps give the literal version.

rules.source: Android ships a trimmed BouncyCastle inside the platform. A copy under the app's own classes is a SECOND, app-controlled crypto provider, and its version is the app's responsibility rather than the platform's.
rules.raises: Read chapter 34 on what the app does with it; a bundled provider is only interesting once you see it registered and used.

rules.source: SpongyCastle exists purely to avoid a name clash with the platform's bundled BouncyCastle. It is the same codebase under a different package.
rules.raises: Treat it as BouncyCastle for vulnerability purposes; the rename does not change the code.

rules.source: Coil 3 moved to the coil3 package so that it could coexist with earlier majors; the unsuffixed package is therefore the earlier line.
rules.raises: Confirm with --refs against Coil artifacts from Maven Central.

rules.source: The coil3 package name marks the third major line.
rules.raises: Same as above.

rules.source: Kotlin has no platform runtime on Android; every Kotlin app carries the stdlib in its own DEX.
rules.raises: META-INF/*.kotlin_module and kotlin/*.kotlin_builtins carry metadata that narrows the compiler version. See README section 3.7 technique 5.

rules.source: Both the full and the 'lite' Android runtime use this package.
rules.raises: Lite and full are different artifacts with the same package. Check whether GeneratedMessageLite or GeneratedMessageV3 is the base class present; that tells you which one, and it changes what the wire format looks like when you get to lab 03.

rules.source: Protobuf is the single most frequently shaded Java library, because two SDKs generated against different protobuf runtimes cannot share one.
rules.raises: Count the distinct copies. Three shaded protobuf runtimes in one APK is common and is worth a line in the report on its own.
